title: Screening paper 5
intro: The hardest of the five: speed and minus marking together, about 17 seconds a question. Make one quick pass for the questions you can settle fast, then spend what’s left on the ones you skipped.

questions.stem: With the committee acting as one body, choose the words that fill both blanks in formal English: “The audit committee ___ approved the internal audit plan, and ___ minutes go out on Monday.”

options.text: have … its
has … their
has … its
have … it’s

questions.reason: A committee acting as one body takes a singular verb and a singular pronoun, so ‘has … its’. ‘Have … its’ and ‘has … their’ switch number halfway through, and ‘it’s’ means ‘it is’.

questions.stem: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to ‘mandatory’ as it is used here: “Attending the induction session is mandatory for every new article.”

options.text: Compulsory
Formal
Occasional
Optional

questions.reason: ‘Mandatory’ means required, so its opposite is ‘optional’: you may choose. ‘Compulsory’ means the same as mandatory, and ‘formal’ and ‘occasional’ describe something else.

questions.stem: Choose the words that fill both blanks: “The client’s office stays open ___ 7 pm, so please send me the final scanned file ___ 6 pm.”

options.text: until … by
by … until
until … until
by … by

questions.reason: ‘Until’ says how long something goes on (the office stays open up to 7 pm); ‘by’ sets a deadline for one action (send it no later than 6 pm). Sending a file is a single act, so ‘until 6 pm’ doesn’t fit.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly written sentence.

options.text: Neither the stores clerks nor the plant head have replied.
Neither the plant head nor the stores clerks has replied.
Neither the plant head or the stores clerks have replied.
Neither the stores clerks nor the plant head has replied.

questions.reason: With ‘neither … nor’ the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it: ‘the plant head has’, so A’s ‘have’ is wrong. In B the nearer subject is ‘the stores clerks’, which needs ‘have’, and C pairs ‘neither’ with ‘or’ instead of ‘nor’.

questions.stem: Which sentence has no needless repetition of meaning?

options.text: Kindly revert back on the stock figures by Monday.
The final outcome of the review is still awaited.
Please send the signed letter back to us by Monday.
Let us repeat the cash count again tomorrow.

questions.reason: ‘Revert’ already means ‘go back’ (at work, ‘reply’), an outcome is already final, and ‘repeat’ already means ‘do again’. In C, ‘back’ is needed: ‘send’ alone doesn’t say the letter is being returned.

questions.stem: Read: “Many small businesses run personal and business spending through one bank account. At the year-end nobody can tell which payments belong in the accounts, so owners spend days sorting statements and still miss some expenses or claim them twice. ___” Which sentence ends the paragraph best?

options.text: So most owners file their returns late every year.
A separate business account from day one avoids most of this.
Banks now offer many kinds of current accounts for small businesses.
Sorting old statements is a useful habit.

questions.reason: The paragraph sets out a problem and its cost, so it ends best with the fix. ‘File late every year’ claims more than the paragraph shows, the line about banks drifts off the topic, and calling the sorting ‘a useful habit’ misses that it is the problem.

questions.stem: One client sent one letter. Choose the correctly written sentence.

options.text: We received the clients letter, but it’s seal was missing.
We received the client’s letter, but it’s seal was missing.
We received the client’s letter, but its seal was missing.
We received the clients’ letter, but its seal was missing.

questions.reason: One client owns the letter, so ‘client’s’; ‘clients’’ would mean several clients. The possessive ‘its’ never takes an apostrophe: ‘it’s’ means ‘it is’.

questions.stem: Choose the word that fills the blank: “We can sign off the stock report only after the ___ of the count.”

options.text: completion
complete
completely
completed

questions.reason: After ‘the’ and before ‘of’ the sentence needs a noun: ‘the completion of the count’. ‘Complete’ and ‘completed’ are verb or adjective forms, and ‘completely’ is an adverb.

questions.stem: Read: “Last year the expense-claims desk took about 6 minutes to check a claim. Now it takes about 4, and its error rate has not risen.” Which conclusion fits these figures best?

options.text: The desk checks each claim faster and no less accurately.
Fewer claims must be reaching the desk this year.
The desk now makes a third fewer errors than it did last year.
The desk now checks each claim less carefully.

questions.reason: Less time per claim with no rise in the error rate means the desk has become more efficient. The figures are per claim, so they say nothing about how many claims arrive; it is the time, not the errors, that fell by a third; and an error rate that hasn’t risen argues against ‘less carefully’.

questions.stem: A client’s cash book shows ₹2,60,000 paid out, marked only ‘advance’. Which line is best for your query to their accountant?

options.text: We’ll have to report this advance unless you explain it today.
Why was such a large amount paid in cash without approval?
Advances like this aren’t allowed, so please reverse the entry.
What was this advance for? Please send its approval and receipt.

questions.reason: A good query asks for the facts and the documents without judging the entry first. Threatening to report it and asking why it had no approval both assume a problem you haven’t found yet, and an article doesn’t tell a client to reverse entries.

questions.stem: Tejas Tools Pvt Ltd makes credit sales of ₹10.95 crore a year, spread evenly over 365 days. Its debtor days fall from 48 to 36. By how much do its average receivables fall?

options.text: ₹12 lakh
₹36 lakh
₹1.08 crore
₹1.44 crore

questions.reason: Receivables are one day’s credit sales times the debtor days, so the fall is 12 days of sales. ₹1.08 crore and ₹1.44 crore are the new and old receivables, not the fall, and ₹12 lakh stops at the 12 days, without multiplying them by a day’s sales of ₹3 lakh.
questions.working: One day’s sales = 10.95 crore ÷ 365 = ₹3 lakh. Fall in days = 48 − 36 = 12. Fall in receivables = 12 × 3 = ₹36 lakh (₹1.44 crore before, ₹1.08 crore after).

questions.stem: The interest rate on Devika Agro’s working-capital loan goes up from 12% a year to 15% a year. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It rose by 25 percentage points.
It rose by 3%, measured on the old rate.
It rose by 3 percentage points, a rise of 20%.
It rose by 3 percentage points, a rise of 25%.

questions.reason: The gap between two rates is in percentage points (15 − 12 = 3); the rise measured on the old rate is a per cent (3 ÷ 12 = 25%). 20% divides by the new rate, and ‘3% of the old rate’ would take it only to 12.36%.

questions.stem: The table shows three purchases of one item in April 2026. What is the weighted average cost per unit?
questions.reason: Weight each rate by its units: total cost ÷ total units. ₹45.00 averages the three rates as if every lot were the same size, ₹46.00 is the rate of the biggest lot, and ₹44.50 is halfway between the lowest and highest rates.

questions.stem: Kosha Stationers buys a printer cartridge for ₹1,440 and prices it at a mark-up of 25% on cost. What is its profit as a percentage of the selling price?
questions.reason: A mark-up is measured on cost and a margin on the selling price, so the same ₹360 is a smaller share of the bigger figure. 25% is the mark-up itself, 33.3% uses 25 ÷ 75 (the rule for turning a margin into a mark-up), and 80% is the cost’s share of the price.

questions.stem: Riya puts ₹40,000 into a savings scheme that pays 10% a year, compounded yearly. How much interest does she earn in the third year alone?
questions.reason: Each year’s interest is earned on the amount at the start of that year, which has grown twice by then. ₹4,000 is simple interest, ₹4,400 is the second year’s interest, and ₹13,240 is the interest of all three years.

questions.stem: Seven trainees can scan and index a client’s old records in 20 days. After 4 days, 7 more trainees join, all working at the same pace. How many more days will the job take?

options.text: 8 days
10 days
12 days
16 days

questions.reason: Count the work in trainee-days and take off what is already done. 10 days forgets the first 4 days’ work, 12 days counts from the start (4 + 8) instead of from when they join, and 16 days ignores the seven who joined.
questions.working: Whole job = 7 × 20 = 140 trainee-days. Done in 4 days = 7 × 4 = 28. Left = 140 − 28 = 112. With 14 trainees: 112 ÷ 14 = 8 days.

questions.stem: An office room is 7.5 m long and 6 m wide. New flooring costs ₹850 a square metre. What does it cost to floor the room?
questions.reason: Flooring is priced by area, length × width. ₹22,950 uses the perimeter, ₹11,475 adds the two sides, and ₹35,700 takes 7 × 6 instead of 7.5 × 6.

questions.stem: A firm has 120 articles: 78 have worked on GST returns, 54 on income-tax returns and 30 on both. How many have done neither?
questions.reason: The 30 who did both are counted in both groups, so take them off once to get those who did at least one. 102 is that ‘at least one’ figure, 48 takes the 30 off twice, and 12 would be the overlap only if every article had done at least one.

questions.stem: Each archive box gets a code of three different letters from A, B, C, D, E, F and G. Order matters, so ABC and CBA are different codes. How many codes are possible?
questions.reason: Seven letters for the first place, six left for the second, five for the third. 35 ignores the order, 343 lets letters repeat, and 5,040 arranges all seven letters.

questions.stem: With its monthly stationery budget, an office can buy 60 cartons of paper at ₹450 a carton. If the price rises to ₹540 a carton, how many cartons will the same budget buy?
questions.reason: The budget is fixed, so price × cartons stays the same: a higher price buys fewer. 72 scales the wrong way, 48 cuts the cartons by 20% because the price rose by 20%, and 10 is how many fewer you get.

questions.stem: Which number in this series is wrong? 3, 7, 14, 18, 36, 42, 80
questions.reason: The steps alternate: add 4, then double (3, 7, 14, 18, 36). So the next term is 36 + 4 = 40, and 40 × 2 = 80 confirms it.

questions.stem: Choose the pair that has the same relationship as Salary : Employee.

options.text: Interest : Lender
Rent : Tenant
Tax : Taxpayer
Discount : Seller

questions.reason: A salary is paid to the employee, and interest is paid to the lender. The tenant and the taxpayer pay rent and tax rather than receive them, and the seller gives the discount.

questions.stem:
Statements: All laptops are tagged items. Some tagged items are leased.
Conclusions:
I. Some leased items are laptops.
II. No leased item is a laptop.
Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Only I follows
Only II follows
Both I and II follow
Neither I nor II follows
Either I or II follows

questions.reason: Neither conclusion is certain alone: the leased tagged items may or may not include laptops. But I and II are exact opposites, so one of them must be true: either I or II follows. ‘Neither’ is the trap.

questions.stem: In an exam merit list, Vir is 9th from the top. Sohan is 3 places below Vir, and Ira is 5 places above Sohan. What is Ira’s rank?

options.text: 1st
7th
11th
17th

questions.reason: ‘Below’ adds places and ‘above’ takes them off: Sohan is 12th, so Ira is 7th. 17th adds both moves, 1st takes off both, and 11th turns both the wrong way.

questions.stem: The pantry is 40 m north of the reception. The server room is 40 m east of the pantry. Where is the reception from the server room?

options.text: North-east
North-west
South-west
South-east

questions.reason: The server room is 40 m north and 40 m east of the reception, so it lies north-east of the reception. Seen from the server room, the reception is the other way: south-west. North-east answers the question the wrong way round.
questions.working: Reception at (0, 0); pantry at (0, 40); server room at (40, 40). From the server room to the reception: 40 m south and 40 m west, so south-west.

questions.stem: Navneet is Dhruv’s parent, and Dhruv is Mansi’s father. How is Navneet related to Mansi?

options.text: Grandfather, on the father’s side
Grandfather or grandmother, on the father’s side
Grandmother, on the father’s side
Uncle or aunt, on the father’s side

questions.reason: Navneet is the parent of Mansi’s father, so a grandparent on her father’s side; ‘parent’ and a name give no gender.

questions.stem: Six colleagues sit at a round table, all facing the centre. Omkar sits opposite Meher. Tushar sits to Meher’s immediate left. Urvi sits between Tushar and Omkar. Leela does not sit next to Meher. Siddhant takes the last seat. Who sits to Siddhant’s immediate right?

options.text: Meher
Omkar
Urvi
Leela

questions.reason: Going round to the left from Meher: Tushar, Urvi, Omkar (opposite her), then two seats, the second of them next to Meher. Leela can’t sit next to Meher, so she takes the first and Siddhant the second, with Meher on his left and Leela on his right.
questions.working: Seats in order to the left from Meher: Meher, Tushar, Urvi, Omkar, Leela, Siddhant (back to Meher). Facing the centre, Siddhant’s left neighbour is Meher and his right neighbour is Leela.

questions.stem: Argument: “Sales rose 15% in the three months after we changed our logo, so the logo brought in the extra sales.” What is the main flaw?

options.text: It treats a later rise as proof that the change caused it.
It looks at sales, when profit is the figure that really matters.
It assumes a logo can never affect sales.
A 15% rise is too small to show anything.

questions.reason: Coming after something is not the same as being caused by it: prices, the season or a new product could explain the rise. The argument assumes the logo can affect sales, not that it can’t, and the size of the rise isn’t the problem.

questions.stem:
What is Gauri’s age?
I. Gauri is 4 years older than Sunil.
II. Sunil is half as old as Charvi.
Which statements, if any, are enough to answer the question?

options.text: Statement I alone is enough, but II alone is not
Statement II alone is enough, but I alone is not
Each statement alone is enough
Both statements together are enough, but neither alone is
Even both statements together are not enough

questions.reason: Together they only link three ages: Gauri = Sunil + 4 and Sunil = Charvi ÷ 2. With no age actually given, Gauri could be 14 (Charvi 20) or 19 (Charvi 30). Two links between three unknowns can’t fix any of them.
questions.working: Charvi 20 gives Sunil 10 and Gauri 14; Charvi 30 gives Sunil 15 and Gauri 19. Both fit I and II, so the age is not fixed.

questions.stem: In a code, CAB is written as 6 and DEAL as 22. Using the same rule, what is FILE?
questions.reason: Each word is the sum of its letters’ places in the alphabet: C3 + A1 + B2 = 6 and D4 + E5 + A1 + L12 = 22. Multiplying the places fits CAB but not DEAL, which is how 3,240 traps you.

questions.stem: Mr Sethi, who owns Sethi Hardware, takes paint costing ₹6,500 from the shop for his home. Ignore GST. Which entry records this?

options.text: Debit Drawings, credit Purchases, ₹6,500
Debit Drawings, credit Sales, ₹6,500
Debit Purchases, credit Drawings, ₹6,500
Debit Capital, credit Cash, ₹6,500

questions.reason: Goods the owner takes are drawings, at cost, and they leave the stock bought for sale, so Purchases is credited. Nothing was sold and no cash moved, so Sales and Cash are wrong.

questions.stem: A ₹42,000 cheque from a customer, Lata Traders, is dishonoured after being banked and recorded. The bank charges ₹300, which the business will recover from Lata Traders. Which entry records this?

options.text: Debit Lata Traders ₹42,000, Bank charges ₹300; credit Bank ₹42,300
Debit Bank ₹42,000; credit Lata Traders ₹42,000
Debit Lata Traders ₹42,300; credit Bank ₹42,300
Debit Sales ₹42,000; credit Bank ₹42,000

questions.reason: The dishonour undoes the receipt, so the customer owes again and the bank balance falls; the charges go to the customer too, since the business will recover them. A would be right only if the business bore the charges itself.
questions.working: Lata Traders = 42,000 + 300 = ₹42,300 debit. Bank = ₹42,300 credit (the cheque reversed plus the charges).

questions.stem: In 2025–26, Meghna Plastics Pvt Ltd charges ₹6 lakh of depreciation in its books; tax depreciation on the same assets is ₹10 lakh. At a 25% tax rate, what does this year’s difference create under AS 22?

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹1 lakh
A deferred tax liability of ₹4 lakh
Nothing: it is a permanent difference
A deferred tax liability of ₹1 lakh

questions.reason: Claiming more depreciation for tax now means more tax later, when the difference reverses: a timing difference that creates a deferred tax liability at the tax rate. ₹4 lakh forgets the rate, and an asset is the wrong direction.
questions.working: Timing difference = 10 − 6 = ₹4 lakh. Deferred tax liability = 4 × 25% = ₹1 lakh.

questions.stem: At 31 March 2026, Saanvi Foods Pvt Ltd holds these. Which one is a cash equivalent under AS 3?

options.text: A fixed deposit made on 1 July 2025, maturing on 30 June 2026
A fixed deposit made on 10 March 2026, maturing on 20 May 2026
Listed equity shares bought on 16 March 2026, to be sold in April
A loan to an employee, repayable in May 2026

questions.reason: A cash equivalent is a short-term, highly liquid investment with little risk of a change in value, normally maturing within three months of the date it was made. The July deposit ran for twelve months when made, shares can change in value however soon you sell them, and a staff loan is a receivable.

questions.stem: Pallav Traders counted its closing stock at 31 March 2026 as ₹4,80,000; the right figure was ₹4,30,000. What is the effect on its 2025–26 accounts?

options.text: Cost of goods sold too high, profit too low
Only the balance sheet is wrong; profit is right
Cost of goods sold and profit both too high
Cost of goods sold too low, profit too high

questions.reason: Closing stock is taken off in working out the cost of goods sold, so stock counted ₹50,000 too high makes that cost ₹50,000 too low and the profit ₹50,000 too high. The balance sheet’s stock is wrong as well.
questions.working: Error = 4,80,000 − 4,30,000 = ₹50,000. Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases − closing stock, so it is ₹50,000 too low and profit ₹50,000 too high.

questions.stem: Toral Mills Ltd has long-term borrowings of ₹36 crore, share capital of ₹10 crore and reserves of ₹14 crore. What is its debt-equity ratio, and what does it show?

options.text: 0.67 : 1; it uses less borrowed money than owners’ funds
1.5 : 1; it uses more borrowed money than owners’ funds
1.5 : 1; it holds more cash than its business needs
3.6 : 1; it uses far more borrowed money than owners’ funds

questions.reason: Equity means the owners’ funds, share capital plus reserves. A ratio above 1 means more borrowed money than owners’ money: higher financial leverage and higher financial risk. 3.6 leaves out the reserves, 0.67 turns the ratio upside down, and the ratio says nothing about cash.

questions.stem: Jasmit Engineering Pvt Ltd has equity of ₹1 crore and a long-term loan of ₹50 lakh. It earns ₹27 lakh before interest and tax and pays ₹6 lakh of interest. What is its return on capital employed?
questions.reason: ROCE compares the profit earned for all long-term providers of money (before interest and tax) with all the long-term money used, equity and loan together. 27% divides by equity alone, 14% takes interest off first, and 21% does both.
questions.working: Capital employed = 1 crore + 50 lakh = ₹150 lakh. ROCE = 27 ÷ 150 × 100 = 18%.

questions.stem: To decide where to focus, an audit team first studies a new client’s business and controls to find where its accounts could be materially wrong. Which SA covers this work?

options.text: SA 230
SA 300
SA 315
SA 520

questions.reason: SA 315 covers identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement by understanding the entity, its environment and its internal control. SA 300 is planning, SA 230 audit documentation and SA 520 analytical procedures.

questions.stem: You want to check that the sales recorded in a client’s sales register really took place. Which test fits best?

options.text: Check register entries against invoices and dispatch notes
Pick dispatch notes and find each one in the sales register
Compare this year’s monthly sales with last year’s
Recalculate the GST on a sample of invoices

questions.reason: To test occurrence, start from the record and look for proof that each sale happened. Starting from dispatch notes runs the other way and tests completeness (every sale recorded); the comparison and the GST check test other things.

questions.stem: Orvi Chemicals Ltd’s finance head signs a letter to the auditor: all the stock at 31 March 2026 is the company’s and fairly valued. How does SA 580 treat this letter?

options.text: As enough evidence on its own, since a senior manager signed it
As not audit evidence at all, as management wrote it
As stronger evidence than the auditor’s own stock count
As audit evidence that still needs other evidence on the stock

questions.reason: Written representations are necessary audit evidence, but on their own they are not sufficient appropriate evidence on the matters they cover. The auditor still needs the count, the costing and the ownership records.

questions.stem: Ekansh Electricals Ltd closes its books on 31 March 2026; its Board approves them on 25 May. On 20 April, a customer owing ₹8 lakh, already struggling at the year-end, is declared insolvent. How does AS 4 treat this?

options.text: As an adjusting event: write down the 2025–26 receivable
As a non-adjusting event, so only disclosed, not adjusted
As a prior period item, corrected in the 2026–27 accounts
Ignored, since it happened after 31 March

questions.reason: The insolvency, known before the accounts are approved, gives evidence about a condition that already existed at 31 March: the receivable was not fully recoverable. That makes it an adjusting event, so the 2025–26 accounts are adjusted.

questions.stem: Under GST, which of these is a zero-rated supply?

options.text: A supply that is exempt from GST
Goods sold by a dealer in Maharashtra to a buyer in Karnataka
Goods supplied to an SEZ unit for its authorised operations
Any supply made to an SEZ unit, whatever its use

questions.reason: Exports, and supplies to an SEZ developer or unit for its authorised operations, are zero-rated: the supplier keeps its input tax credit or gets a refund. Not every supply to an SEZ qualifies, an exempt supply carries no credit, and a sale between two States is taxed under IGST.

questions.stem: In tax year 2026–27, Ketaki Exports Pvt Ltd pays ₹1,60,000 as fees for professional services to a resident consultant who has given a PAN. How much tax must it deduct at source?

options.text: Nil

questions.reason: Fees for professional services of more than ₹50,000 in the year bear TDS at 10% on the whole amount, not only on the part above ₹50,000 (₹11,000). ₹3,200 uses the 2% rate for fees for technical services.

questions.stem: Varsha Castings Ltd’s accounts team has finished the 2025–26 financial statements. Under the Companies Act, 2013, what must happen before they are signed and sent to the auditors?

options.text: Adoption by the shareholders at the AGM
Approval by the statutory auditor
Filing with the Registrar of Companies
Approval by the Board of Directors

questions.reason: The Board approves the financial statements before they are signed on its behalf and submitted to the auditors. The shareholders adopt them later, at the annual general meeting (AGM), and filing with the Registrar comes after that.

questions.stem: Mridul Ceramics Ltd has sued a supplier for ₹20 lakh. At 31 March 2026 its lawyers think it will probably win; the case is pending. Under AS 29, does it record the ₹20 lakh as an asset?

options.text: Yes, because the inflow is probable
No, not even after a final judgment in its favour
Yes, half of it, as the outcome is uncertain
No, not until the inflow is virtually certain

questions.reason: A contingent asset is not recognised. Once the inflow becomes virtually certain, the asset is no longer contingent and is recognised then. ‘Probable’ is enough for a provision, not for an asset.

questions.stem: A client’s accountant emails you a payroll file that belongs to another company. What do you do first?

options.text: Forward it to that company so it reaches them quickly
Close the file and tell both the sender and your senior
Read it through first, so you can tell the sender exactly what was in it
Delete it quietly and say nothing, so nobody is embarrassed

questions.reason: Someone else’s confidential data has reached the wrong person: stop, report it and let the firm deal with it under its policy. Forwarding it spreads it further, reading it through exposes more of someone else’s data than you need to, and deleting it silently hides an incident others need to know about.

questions.stem: Your senior wants 25 expense vouchers picked at random. A colleague says, “Skip the handwritten ones; they always have problems.” What do you do?

options.text: Skip them, so there are fewer exceptions to explain
Pick only handwritten ones, since that is where the problems are
Pick as planned, handwritten ones included; note what you find
Pick all 25 from March, since the year-end is riskiest

questions.reason: Leaving out the items most likely to show problems hides the very errors the test exists to find, and picking only from March isn’t a random pick from the year. Pick as planned; if handwritten vouchers look riskier, tell your senior, since extra testing is their call.

questions.stem: The client’s sales head gives you only the total of customer discounts and refuses the customer-wise list as confidential. What do you do?

options.text: Accept the total, since the list is confidential
Agree the total to the discount account in the ledger, and stop there
Ask someone in the sales team to send you the list quietly
Offer to view it at their office; if refused, tell your senior

questions.reason: Confidentiality is a reason to handle the data carefully, not to go without it: the audit team keeps it confidential anyway. Matching the total to the ledger checks the arithmetic, not whether each discount was allowed, and going round the sales head breaks the client’s trust. A refusal limits the audit, so your senior must know.

questions.stem: Your senior wants a ₹6 lakh government grant towards a new machine shown in full as this year’s income. From your reading of AS 12, you think it should be set against the machine’s cost or spread over its life. What do you do?

options.text: Show your senior the grant letter and AS 12, and discuss it
Book it in full as income, since your senior is more experienced
Change it in your working paper without telling anyone
Do whatever the client’s accountant prefers

questions.reason: Raise a technical doubt politely, with the grant letter and the standard, so it can be settled; your senior, or the manager after them, decides. Going along silently, changing it quietly and handing the decision to the client all leave the doubt unsettled.

questions.stem: The client’s accountant is behind schedule and asks you to pass the year-end entries in their software yourself. What do you do?

options.text: Pass them, since it saves everyone time before the deadline
Pass them, but leave them out of your working papers
Politely decline (entries are their job) and tell your senior
Ask your senior to pass them instead

questions.reason: Recording transactions is management’s responsibility. If anyone on the audit team, you or your senior, passes the client’s entries, the team ends up auditing its own work, which threatens independence. Decline politely and let your senior decide what help is allowed.

questions.stem: You’re working on a client’s ledger on your firm laptop in a café and must step away for two minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Minimise the ledger window so nobody can read it
Lock the screen or take the laptop with you
Ask the person at the next table to watch it
Leave it, since you’ll be back soon

questions.reason: An unlocked laptop can be read, copied or taken in seconds, so lock it or carry it, even for two minutes. A minimised window opens with one click, and a stranger is no safeguard for client data.

questions.stem: In a review meeting, the partner asks the GST rate on the client’s main product. You don’t remember it. What do you say?

options.text: Give the likeliest rate, so you don’t look unprepared
Quote the rate in last year’s working papers, since rates rarely change
Ask a colleague to message you the rate during the meeting
Admit you don’t remember it, then check and reply the same day

questions.reason: A wrong figure said with confidence does more harm than an honest ‘I don’t remember; I’ll check.’ An old file may show a rate that has since changed, and a rate passed to you quietly is still unchecked.

questions.stem: The client’s purchase manager asks for your draft list of control gaps before your senior has reviewed it. What do you do?

options.text: Say it comes after review, and tell your senior about the request
Send it, since the gaps are in the manager’s own area
Read it out on a call, so nothing is in writing
Send only the minor points for now, and hold back the serious ones

questions.reason: Draft points can change after review, and sharing them early can mislead the client or alert them before testing is done. Findings go to the client after review, through your senior, in writing or on a call.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the GST Council?

options.text: It collects GST from registered businesses
It audits the GST returns and accounts of registered businesses
It decides appeals in GST disputes
It recommends GST rates and exemptions to the Centre and States

questions.reason: The GST Council is a joint forum of the Centre and the States, chaired by the Union Finance Minister. It recommends rates, exemptions, thresholds and model laws; it does not collect tax, decide appeals or audit businesses.
